content: Breast self-examination (BSE) is a simple technique that can help in the early detection of some types of breast cancer, but it is not a reliable standalone method. When performed correctly and consistently, BSE may assist in identifying abnormalities, but it should not replace proven screening methods such as mammography, which are more effective in detecting breast cancer. The process of BSE involves carefully feeling the breasts to detect any distortions, lumps, or swelling. Here are the steps to perform a BSE: 1. Stand in front of a mirror with your upper body exposed. Place your hands on your hips and visually inspect your breasts for any signs of dimpling, swelling, redness, or soreness. Repeat this inspection with your arms raised above your head. 2. While standing, use your fingers to palpate your breasts, feeling for any lumps or irregularities. Use the pads of your fingers rather than poking with the tips, and ensure you examine both the superficial tissue just beneath the skin and the deeper tissue within the breast. 3. Cover the entire breast area during the examination. One method is to divide the breast into quadrants and palpate each quadrant thoroughly. Don’t forget to examine the axillary tail, which extends toward the armpit. 4. Repeat the palpation process while lying down, as this position can help spread the breast tissue more evenly. 5. Check the nipples and the area beneath them. Gently squeeze each nipple to check for any discharge. A structured approach to BSE is known as the Seven P's method, which includes the following: Position: Inspect the breasts visually and palpate them in front of a mirror with your arms in various positions. Perform the examination lying down, first with a pillow under one shoulder, then the other, and finally lying flat. Perimeter: Examine the entire breast, including the nipple, the axillary tail extending into the armpit, and nearby lymph nodes. Palpation: Use the pads of your fingers to palpate the breast without lifting your fingers as you move across the tissue. Pressure: Apply varying levels of pressure—light, moderate, and firm—to feel different layers of breast tissue. Pattern: Use a consistent pattern for examination, such as the vertical strip pattern (moving fingers up and down), the pie-wedge pattern (starting at the nipple and moving outward), or the circular pattern (moving in concentric circles from the nipple outward). Be sure to palpate into the axilla as well. Practice: Regularly practice BSE to become familiar with the normal feel of your breast tissue, which will help you recognize any changes. A healthcare provider can provide feedback on your technique. Plan: Know what steps to take if you detect any changes in your breast tissue. Be aware of your family history of breast cancer and follow your healthcare provider’s recommendations for mammography. For premenopausal women, BSE is best performed at the same stage of the menstrual cycle each month, ideally just after the end of the last period when the breasts are least likely to be swollen or tender. Postmenopausal women should perform BSE once a month, perhaps on the same day each month for consistency. It is important to note that approximately 80% of lumps discovered through BSE are benign. However, any abnormality detected during a BSE should be promptly reported to a doctor. While many breast cancers are first identified by women themselves, BSE should be combined with an annual clinical breast examination by a healthcare provider for improved detection accuracy. Women may miss lumps that an expert can identify, which is why learning BSE from a trained professional is recommended. BSE is not a substitute for more reliable diagnostic techniques such as mammography or MRI. For comprehensive and up-to-date information, consult reputable sources such as the Johns Hopkins Breast Cancer Center.
